questions.q: What are the five standard stages of a narrative plot in order?
questions.a: The five stages are: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution. A wrong answer (e.g., listing only beginning, middle, end) reveals the student lacks the precise vocabulary needed for board exam analysis and cannot map the Kabir passage onto a structured framework.

questions.q: In the Kabir biographical excerpt, the author describes Kabir's daily routine and his disciples' curiosity before narrating the specific incident of the weaving demonstration. Which plot stage does this initial description represent, and why?
questions.a: This is the exposition stage because it establishes the setting (Kabir's workshop), the characters (Kabir and disciples), and the background context (Kabir's method of teaching through work). A wrong answer (e.g., calling it rising action) shows the student confuses background setup with the development of conflict.

questions.q: Apply the concept of 'rising action' to the passage: identify two specific events that escalate the disciples' curiosity and lead to the climax.
questions.a: Two events: (1) The disciples observe Kabir weaving silently and ask about the purpose of his unusual pattern. (2) Kabir ignores their questions and continues working, heightening their anticipation. A wrong answer that picks random details indicates the student cannot distinguish between events that build tension and those that are merely descriptive.

questions.q: Analyze how the author uses the narrative technique of 'showing' (describing actions and dialogue) rather than 'telling' (directly stating the moral) during the climax of the incident. What effect does this create?
questions.a: At the climax, the author describes Kabir cutting the woven cloth and distributing pieces, letting the disciples (and readers) infer the lesson on detachment. This creates an experiential realization mirroring Kabir's teaching style. A wrong answer that only identifies the moral without analyzing the technique shows the student misses the author's narrative craft.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the resolution of the passage (the disciples' understanding) is effectively prepared by the preceding narrative structure. Justify your view with evidence.
questions.a: Yes, the resolution is effective because the falling action shows the disciples reflecting on the pieces of cloth, and the resolution ties back to the exposition's mention of Kabir's practical pedagogy. A wrong answer that calls it abrupt or unearned reveals the student has not traced the causal chain from exposition through climax.

questions.q: Create a brief alternative ending for the incident that changes the narrative structure from a linear chronological order to a flashback structure. Write 3-4 sentences showing how the story would begin.
questions.a: A good answer begins in medias res: "Years later, a disciple recalled the day Kabir cut his woven cloth..." then flashes back to the event. A poor answer simply rewrites the same chronological order, showing the student cannot manipulate narrative time.
